# Browser Resolution and Lifecycle

Every Yantra operation that needs a browser — `ask`, `research`, `do`, `run`, `resume`, workflow
recording, and `yantra doctor` — answers "which browser, and is it usable?" the same way. One
resolution decides which executable a run gets and where that answer came from; one local
compatibility check decides whether that executable can do the work; and one process supervisor
accounts for the browser, its profile, and its managed claim when the run ends or fails to start.

This document describes what you can observe and diagnose. `docs/architecture.md`, section "Browser
resolution, compatibility, and process ownership", describes how the seam is composed.

## What It Does

### Picks one browser, with visible provenance

A browser choice is a source — `auto`, `managed`, or `system` — plus an optional absolute executable
path that is legal only with `system`. The choice is taken from the first of these that supplies
one:

1. the selection the invocation supplies;
2. a persisted selection read from `config.yaml`; and
3. `auto`.

Precedence replaces the choice as a whole and never merges it field by field. A selection of
`system` with no path therefore clears a configured custom path rather than inheriting it.

`auto` prefers the single ready Yantra-managed installation under the data directory's `browsers/`
tree. When no managed installation is ready, it discovers an external Chrome or Chromium from the
standard install locations for the host and records the channel it found (`stable`, `beta`, `dev`,
`canary`, `chromium`, or `unknown`). Discovery and resolution read the filesystem and the binary's
version metadata only: nothing here launches a browser, contacts a version server, or downloads
anything.

Two refusals are deliberate and matter when you are diagnosing a surprise:

- A managed record that exists but is corrupt, disagrees with the on-disk layout, or points at a
  missing or unreadable executable stops `auto` with remediation. It does not silently fall through
  to an external Chrome, because running a different browser than the machine is set up around is
  exactly the outcome this contract removes.
- An explicit `system` selection never falls back to the managed tree, and an explicit `managed`
  selection never falls back to external discovery.

Resolution does not check compatibility and does not launch. It reports the executable's canonical
path, version, major version, platform, architecture, a stat fingerprint, whether it is
Yantra-managed or external, and why it was chosen (`managed-preferred`, `managed-explicit`,
`system-discovery`, or `custom-path`).

### Decides ownership of a custom path canonically

An explicit executable path must be absolute, and it is legal only with `system`. Ownership is then
decided by where the path really lands after symlinks and junctions are resolved, not by how it was
spelled:

- A path that genuinely resolves inside the managed root is treated as managed-owned. It must be the
  exact ready installation; a path into an orphan `installation-*` tree, or any path inside the root
  when no managed installation is ready, is refused.
- A path whose lexical position and canonical position disagree — a symlink or junction that crosses
  the managed root boundary in either direction — is refused as a selection error rather than
  followed.
- A path that resolves outside the managed root is an ordinary external browser, read and launched
  but never written to or deleted.

### Has no minimum Chrome version

Yantra declares no minimum Chrome major and no maximum. Support is a table of primitives Yantra
actually needs, each checked locally against the actual binary:

| Primitive              | Needed for                                                                        | Required by           |
| ---------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------- |
| `pipe-version`         | Reading the browser version over the CDP pipe transport Yantra drives it through. | automation, recording |
| `runtime-evaluate`     | Every observation and every action evaluates JavaScript in the page.              | automation, recording |
| `dom-handles`          | The locator engine collects element handles and releases them again.              | automation, recording |
| `click-replace`        | Filling a field that already has a value replaces it rather than appending.       | automation, recording |
| `frame-token`          | Addressing actions inside non-main frames, and only their live owning frame.      | automation, recording |
| `popup-session`        | A site-opened popup owning its own page and CDP session, cleaned up with it.      | automation, recording |
| `recorder-binding`     | Receiving in-page events through a CDP binding on the recording session.          | recording             |
| `recorder-preload`     | Installing the recorder overlay before page scripts run.                          | recording             |
| `recorder-page-domain` | Tracking navigation and frame attachment through the Page domain.                 | recording             |

`puppeteer-core@25.10.0` was tested against Chrome build `152.0.7977.75`. That build is a recorded
baseline, not a floor and not a target. A newer Stable build is the normal case: it passes the same
primitive checks and its result is reported as `capability-checked`. A build that matches the tested
pairing exactly is reported as `tested`. Neither value is a warning, and a build outside the tested
pairing produces no per-run notice — only a structured log entry and the provenance shown by
`yantra doctor`.

### Checks compatibility in a throwaway session

There is exactly one compatibility check, and it always runs the same way. It launches its own
isolated headless session against the executable being judged, with its own ephemeral profile, and
closes that session and removes that profile on success and on failure alike — including when a
primitive throws partway through. It is never the session you are about to work in.

The check exercises each required primitive in dependency order against `about:blank` and in-memory
documents it builds itself. It does not open a URL you supplied, does not touch a personal Chrome
profile, does not capture a screenshot, and does not contact the network. A primitive gets 15
seconds; session startup gets 30. A primitive whose prerequisite failed is reported as not run,
naming that prerequisite, so the output points at the one real cause rather than a cascade.

For an ordinary task the check runs only when no valid cached evidence exists, so you pay for one
extra short-lived browser per executable identity, not one per run.

### Names the failure class

A refusal is one of three kinds, and they have different repairs:

- **Missing browser runtime libraries.** The browser could not start because shared objects it needs
  are absent — the common failure on a minimal Linux host or container image. Remediation is
  rendered from the installation's own `deb.deps` file, so it names the actual package list, for
  example `sudo apt-get install -y libnss3 libgbm1`, and includes the loader output. When no
  `deb.deps` is available the message says the runtime library packages for your distribution are
  missing without inventing names.
- **Capability failure.** The browser started but one or more required primitives did not work. The
  message names each failing primitive. It never implies a version mismatch alone caused it.
- **Launch environment.** Everything else that prevented startup, reported with the executable path
  and the underlying detail.

Yantra classes all three as environment failures. Where the surface reports an exit code for them —
`yantra doctor` and `yantra browser install` — that code is `3`.

### Requires more of a recording browser

Recording needs the automation primitives plus `recorder-binding`, `recorder-preload`, and
`recorder-page-domain`. Evidence is stored per probe profile, so evidence that approved automation
can never approve a recording; recording verifies its own profile before any recorder initialization
or user navigation. The recording browser is started with the recording's own profile directory,
never a personal Chrome profile root.

### Reuses only successful, still-valid evidence

A passing result is stored under the cache directory, in `browser-compatibility/`. The key covers
everything that could change the answer: the canonical executable path, its version, its stat
fingerprint (size, modification time, and filesystem identity), the host platform and architecture,
the pinned driver version, the probe revision, a hash of the declared primitive table, and the probe
profile. Change any of them — replace the binary, upgrade Chrome, move to another machine, change
the driver, add a required primitive — and the old evidence is no longer an answer to the new
question.

Only a passing result is ever reused. A recorded failure is kept for diagnosis but never satisfies a
launch, and a file that is missing, malformed, or describes a different executable is treated as no
evidence at all. Losing the cache costs one more local check; it can never cause a download or an
update.

Startup re-reads the executable after the check and before the launch. If the binary changed while
the check was running, the evidence describes a different file, so Yantra re-resolves and re-verifies
against the build that is actually there.

### Leaves nothing behind

A startup that fails at any step undoes exactly what it acquired:

- No browser process survives. A browser that arrives after Yantra has given up waiting is still
  closed and awaited rather than abandoned.
- Only an ephemeral profile that this startup created is removed. A workflow profile or an explicit
  profile directory you own is never deleted by a failed startup. A failed recording startup also
  leaves the recording directory and any draft in place.
- A managed reservation taken before the browser existed is released with the explicit proof that
  nothing was ever spawned under it.

A managed browser's claim is released only after its process tree has verifiably exited. A signal
sent, a `killed` flag, and a Puppeteer disconnect are all requests or transport events, not exits;
only the process exit counts. Shutdown asks politely first, escalates on a bounded schedule, and
terminates the whole tree (`taskkill /T /F` on Windows, with no console window shown). If exit still
cannot be proved, the claim is deliberately kept and a typed process error is raised, because
releasing on a guess would let a later operation delete a tree a live Chrome still holds open.

## How to Use It

Nothing has to be configured for the common case. Ordinary commands resolve, verify, and launch a
browser on their own:

```console
yantra ask "what changed in the release notes"
yantra run <workflow-name>
```

`auto` is the default answer when nothing has been configured, and what it finds is still yours to
control: install the Yantra-managed build and `auto` prefers it; leave it uninstalled and `auto`
discovers your system Chrome or Chromium. To persist a different source, or to override one
invocation, see [Browser Selection and Diagnostics](browser-selection-and-diagnostics.md).

To acquire the managed build, see [Managed Stable Installation](managed-stable-installation.md); it
owns the consent, download, and verification path.

```console
yantra browser install
```

To see which browser a run would actually use, and whether it has been checked on this machine:

```console
yantra doctor
yantra doctor --json
```

To move where the managed tree and the rest of Yantra's data live, preview first:

```console
yantra config data-dir /new/path --dry-run
yantra config data-dir /new/path
```

## Inputs and Outputs

### `yantra doctor`

Two of doctor's browser checks read this feature's contracts. Both are read-only: doctor reports
what is there and never launches a browser to manufacture a passing result.

| Check                   | Reports                                                                                                                 |
| ----------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `browser.selection`     | The resolver's actual selection — version, ownership, and canonical path, with the source, origin, and reason it chose. |
| `browser.compatibility` | Cached local evidence for that browser under the `automation` profile.                                                  |

`browser.selection` fails with the resolution error's own message, code, and remediation when no
browser can be selected. It uses the one resolution path every launch uses, so it cannot disagree
with what a run will do.

`browser.compatibility` reports these states honestly:

| State        | Status | Meaning                                                                                                                |
| ------------ | ------ | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `passed`     | ok     | Every required primitive was proved, with the pairing (`tested` or `capability-checked`), tested build, and timestamp. |
| `failed`     | error  | Named failing primitives and the failure class, with the check's own remediation.                                      |
| `unverified` | warn   | This browser has not been checked on this machine yet, or no browser was selected at all.                              |
| `stale`      | warn   | The recorded evidence describes a different executable than the one now selected.                                      |

`yantra doctor` exits `3` when any check is an error, and `0` otherwise; warnings do not fail it.

### Resolution error codes

When resolution refuses, the failure carries a code, the selection that was requested, sanitized
local evidence, and one remediation string.

| Code                    | Meaning                                                                                                             |
| ----------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `missing`               | Nothing was found: no managed installation, no discoverable Chrome or Chromium, or no file at an explicit path.     |
| `invalid-selection`     | A malformed selection, a relative or non-`system` executable path, a symlink escape, or a path into an orphan tree. |
| `invalid-executable`    | The file exists but could not be identified as a Chrome or Chromium binary.                                         |
| `managed-state-invalid` | The managed ready record is corrupt, disagrees with the on-disk layout, or names a missing executable.              |
| `unsupported-platform`  | Chrome for Testing publishes no managed build for this platform and architecture.                                   |

A compatibility refusal and a process-accounting failure are separate typed failures, not missing
browsers, because they call for different repairs.

### `yantra config data-dir`

Run with no argument, the command prints the current data directory and where that value came from
(`--json` emits `kind: "config.data-dir"` with `path` and `source`).

Given a target path, relocation is refused before any filesystem change while a Yantra-managed
browser run is active:

```text
data relocation is unavailable while a Yantra-managed browser run is active; stop the running
sessions and retry
```

That refusal exits `3`. On Windows a live managed `chrome.exe` holds its own binary open, so the
move would otherwise fail partway and leave exactly the half-relocated state this prevents.

The managed tree's fate is decided up front, before anything moves, and is reported identically in
human output, `--json`, and `--dry-run`:

| Decision             | When                                               | What happens                                                                                                  |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `absent`             | No managed tree exists, or `--no-move` was passed. | Nothing to relocate.                                                                                          |
| `move`               | Target is on the same volume.                      | The managed tree moves with the data directory.                                                               |
| `drop-and-reinstall` | Target is on a different volume.                   | The tree is excluded from the copy, removed at the source only after the relocation commits, and reinstalled. |

Human output prints `Managed browsers: <decision> - <note>` after the relocation line; the note for a
cross-volume move directs you to run `yantra browser install` afterwards. JSON emits
`kind: "config.data-dir"` carrying `from`, `to`, `move`, and `managedBrowsers` — with `dryRun: true`
for a preview and `status: "relocated"` for a completed move. Hundreds of megabytes of
re-downloadable binaries are never copied across a volume boundary, and the source-side removal is
guarded by canonical containment so it can never reach the parent directory.

## Configuration and Permissions

Managed browser state lives under the resolved data directory:

```text
<data>/browsers/                            the managed tree
<data>/browsers/ready.json                  the single ready pointer
<data>/browsers/operation.json              the exclusive mutation claim
<data>/browsers/coordination/               use reservations and the mutex
<cache>/browser-compatibility/              local compatibility evidence
```

The defaults are `~/.yantra/data` and `~/.yantra/cache`. Both are relocatable, with the ordinary
precedence:

```text
YANTRA_DATA_DIR  > config.yaml paths.data_dir  > <YANTRA_HOME>/data
YANTRA_CACHE_DIR > config.yaml paths.cache_dir > <YANTRA_HOME>/cache
```

`YANTRA_HOME` changes the home used for those fallbacks; it defaults to `~/.yantra` on every
platform. Coordination state sits outside every installation child, so removing one child can never
encompass another or the coordination files. Directories are created owner-only (`0700`) and records
written owner-only (`0600`) where the platform supports POSIX modes.

Only the ready pointer makes a managed installation selectable. Any other `installation-*` child of
the managed root is an orphan by construction — never an alternate version, never selectable, and
never a blocker for ordinary use. This feature only enumerates orphans; it deletes nothing.

The persisted selection this feature's resolver reads lives in the `browser` block of `config.yaml`
and is written only by `yantra browser use` or the ordinary configuration key surface; see
[Browser Selection and Diagnostics](browser-selection-and-diagnostics.md). No new permission,
credential, or authentication path is involved. Browser selection is not consent to use your personal
browsing data: the existing refusal of real Chrome profile roots is unchanged, and external browsers
and their profiles are read and launched but never modified.

Resolution, the compatibility check, the evidence cache, session and recorder startup, `doctor`, and
`config data-dir` never resolve a Stable build, download anything, or check for updates.

## Limitations

- `yantra browser update` does not exist. The remediation strings that name it are guidance text from
  the current code, not a command you can run. Pinning, rollback, and a selectable version history are
  out of scope by design: one ready pointer names the only selectable managed installation.
- The command surface for every selection this resolver honors — `yantra browser use`, `browser list`,
  `browser check`, and the `--browser` / `--browser-path` flags — is documented in
  [Browser Selection and Diagnostics](browser-selection-and-diagnostics.md) rather than here. This
  document describes the resolution and lifecycle contract those commands drive.
- A compatibility failure inside a task command (`ask`, `research`, `do`, `run`, `resume`) aborts the
  run with the typed failure and its remediation. `yantra doctor`, `yantra browser install`,
  `yantra browser check`, and `yantra config data-dir` map browser environment failures onto the
  documented exit code `3` themselves.
- Compatibility evidence is per machine, per executable identity, and per probe profile. It is not
  shared between hosts, and replacing the binary in place invalidates it.
- The check proves the primitives Yantra needs from a browser. It is not a general Chrome health
  check, and passing it does not predict how a particular website will behave.
- The managed tree is not relocated across volumes. A cross-volume `config data-dir` move removes it
  and requires a fresh `yantra browser install`.
- Recording has no public CLI command; its startup contract is exercised through the core
  `RecordingSession` API.
